questions.q: How does the chapter describe the family?
questions.a: As the fundamental and most ancient unit of any society
o: As the fundamental and most ancient unit of any society
As a newer unit that grew out of the larger community
As a unit found mainly in villages, not in towns and cities
As the largest unit of any society

questions.q: Meera lives in one house with her grandparents, her parents, her father's brother, his wife and their two children. Which type of family is this, as the chapter describes the types?
questions.a: A joint family, because several generations live together
o: A joint family, because several generations live together
A nuclear family, because they all share one house
A nuclear family, because there is only one set of grandparents
A community, because it has more than five members

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A Hindi-speaking girl may call her mother's brother's daughter 'bahan'.
Reason (R): In most Indian languages there is no separate word for 'cousin', because cousins are considered 'brothers' and 'sisters'.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements and use the chapter's descriptions to judge them.
I. A household of a grandmother, her son, his wife and their two children has three generations living together, so it fits the chapter's idea of a joint family.
II. A widowed father living with his two daughters is not a nuclear family, because a nuclear family must have a couple.
III. Tamil has different terms for an elder brother and a younger brother, where English uses the single word 'brother'.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: What is a nuclear family, as the chapter describes it? Give one example of a household that is a nuclear family.
questions.a: A nuclear family is limited to a couple and their children, and sometimes one parent and children. Example: a mother and father living with their two sons (or a mother living alone with her daughter).
s: States that a nuclear family is limited to a couple and their children, or sometimes one parent and children
Gives a correct example, such as parents with their children or one parent with children

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says that English has many more terms for family relationships than Indian languages such as Hindi.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that English does not have many terms for family relationships, while Indian languages have many more; Hindi, for example, has bua, tau, tai, chacha, mausi, nana and nani.
s: Verdict: False
Corrects it: English has few such terms; Indian languages such as Hindi have many more (e.g. chacha, mausi, nana)

questions.q:
Priyanka's mother's sister has a son, Aman, who often stays at Priyanka's home.
(a) What one word would English use for Aman's relation to Priyanka, and what would he usually be called instead in most Indian languages, going by the chapter?
(b) What does the chapter say this way of naming such relatives emphasises?
questions.a: (a) In English Aman is Priyanka's 'cousin'; in most Indian languages there is no word for cousin, so he would be called her 'brother'. (b) It emphasises the deep bonds among all the children in the family.
s: (a) Cousin in English; 'brother' in most Indian languages
(b) It shows the deep bonds among all the children in the family

questions.q:
(a) Which two things does Tiruvalluvar call 'the flower and fruit of family life' in the line that opens the chapter?
(b) Name the two types of family that the chapter places at the two ends of the range of families in India today.
(c) Write one difference between these two types.
questions.a: (a) Love and dharma. (b) Joint families and nuclear families. (c) A joint family has several generations living together (grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, cousins), while a nuclear family is limited to a couple and their children, or one parent and children.
s: (a) Love and dharma
(b) Joint family and nuclear family
(c) One correct difference: several generations together versus only a couple (or one parent) and children

questions.q: The chapter notes that 'quite often, a single word in your mother tongue or regional language requires several words in English to give a precise definition.' (a) Show this using the chapter's Hindi example of Sameer. (b) Show it using the chapter's Hindi example of Rani. (c) Explain why the single English word 'cousin' would not describe Rani precisely.
questions.a: (a) Sameer is called 'chacha', which needs the English words 'father's younger brother' to define. (b) Rani is called 'bahan', and her relation needs the words 'mother's brother's daughter' in English. (c) 'Cousin' could mean the child of any uncle or aunt on either side, so it does not tell whether she is a mother's brother's daughter or some other cousin; the precise description needs several words.
s: (a) Chacha = father's younger brother: one Hindi word, three English words
(b) Rani = mother's brother's daughter, several English words for one relation
(c) Explains that 'cousin' covers many different relations, so it is not precise on its own

questions.q:
A volunteer for a colony festival committee in Pune lists five households.
H1: Mr and Mrs Kulkarni and their daughter.
H2: Mrs Fernandes, a widow, and her two sons.
H3: Grandfather Joshi, his two sons, their two wives and four grandchildren (two children of each son).
H4: Mr and Mrs Rao, Mr Rao's mother and their son.
H5: Mr and Mrs Bhat and their three children.
(a) Which household is a nuclear family made up of one parent and children?
(b) How many people in all live in the households that are nuclear families?
(c) In H3, what are the children of one son to the children of the other son in English, and what would they usually call each other in most Indian languages?
(d) The committee wants to list H4 as a nuclear family 'because it has no uncles, aunts or cousins'. Should it? Justify using the chapter's descriptions.
questions.a: (a) H2, a mother with her two children. (b) H1, H2 and H5 are nuclear: 3 + 3 + 5 = 11 people. (c) In English they are cousins; in most Indian languages there is no word for cousin, so they would call each other brothers and sisters. (d) No. A nuclear family is limited to a couple and their children (or one parent and children), and H4 also has Mr Rao's mother. With a grandmother, parents and a son, three generations live together, which is what the chapter calls a joint family; it does not need uncles, aunts or cousins to be one.
s: (a) H2
(b) Identifies H1, H2, H5 and adds to 11
(c) Cousins in English; brothers and sisters in most Indian languages
(d) Says no: the grandmother makes three generations, which fits a joint family, not the couple-and-children nuclear family

questions.q: According to the chapter, relationships among family members are based on love, care, cooperation and what else?
questions.a: Interdependence

questions.q: The chapter says that the family is also a 'school'. What does it mean by this?
questions.a: Children learn important values such as ahimsa, dana, seva and tyaga in the family.
o: Children learn important values such as ahimsa, dana, seva and tyaga in the family.
Parents must teach every school subject to their children at home, after school hours.
Children go to school only to learn the values of their family.
Every family should run classes for the children of its neighbourhood.

questions.q:
Match each word (Column A) with the meaning the chapter gives for it (Column B).
Column A: 1. dana 2. seva 3. tyaga 4. dharma
Column B: A. sacrifice B. doing our duty C. giving D. service

Assertion (A): Through daily practice, children learn to participate in the life of the household.
Reason (R): In many homes, children also learn some of the traditions and practices their family has followed for generations.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: What does 'cooperation' mean, as the chapter explains it? Give one example of cooperation among members of a family.
questions.a: Cooperation means 'working together'. Example: the whole family cleans the house together before a festival, or one member cooks while another sets out the plates.
s: States that cooperation means working together
Gives a fitting family example of members working together

questions.q:
During Deepa's board exams, her elder brother gives up his evening cricket match every day for a month so that the house stays quiet while she studies.
(a) Which value named in the chapter does his action show most clearly?
(b) Link his action to what the chapter says individuals in a family often do.
questions.a: (a) Tyaga (sacrifice). (b) The chapter says individuals in the family often give up their own needs to take care of the family's needs; he gives up his own cricket so that his sister's need to study is met.
s: (a) Tyaga (sacrifice)
(b) Links it to giving up one's own needs for the family's needs

questions.q:
(a) According to the chapter, what are parents responsible for?
(b) What do children do in the home as they grow up?
(c) What does 'following our dharma' mean, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: (a) Raising their children to become happy individuals and responsible members of society. (b) They take on more responsibilities in the home to help other family members, such as parents, a sister or a brother. (c) Doing our duty.
s: (a) Raising children to be happy individuals and responsible members of society
(b) Taking on more responsibilities at home to help other members
(c) Doing our duty

questions.q: Meena says: 'When I help my younger brother with his homework every evening without being told, I am doing three things the chapter talks about at once: taking on a responsibility as I grow up, cooperating, and learning in the family as a school.' Check Meena's claim against the chapter and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Meena is right. (1) The chapter says that as children grow up they take on more responsibilities in the home to help other members, such as a sister or a brother; helping her brother is such a responsibility. (2) Cooperation means working together, and she and her brother work together on his homework. (3) The chapter calls the family a 'school' where children learn values through daily practice; by helping every day she is practising service and care, so she is learning as well as helping.
s: Verdict: the claim is right, linked to children taking on more responsibilities to help a brother or sister
Shows that it is cooperation, i.e. working together
Shows that daily practice in the family is how values are learnt (the family as a 'school')

questions.q: In the Hussain family of Lucknow, the grandfather breaks his leg. Over the next month the mother takes leave from work to look after him; twelve-year-old Zoya takes over watering the plants and helps her little brother with his reading; the father gives up a trip he had planned with friends; and the grandfather, from his bed, teaches the children an old family recipe. Using the chapter, explain how this family shows (i) interdependence, (ii) children taking on more responsibilities as they grow, (iii) tyaga, and (iv) the passing on of family traditions.
questions.a: (i) Interdependence: the grandfather depends on the others for care, and the others depend on him too, for example to learn the recipe; each member has a role towards the others. (ii) Zoya, as she grows up, takes on the plants and her brother's reading to help other members. (iii) Tyaga: the father gives up his planned trip, and the mother her work time, putting the family's needs before their own. (iv) The grandfather passes on an old family recipe, a practice the family has followed for generations, which the chapter says children learn in many homes.
s: (i) Shows members depending on one another (care for the grandfather, his teaching for the children)
(ii) Zoya's new tasks as a child taking on more responsibilities
(iii) The father giving up his trip (or the mother her work) as tyaga, sacrifice of own needs
(iv) The recipe as a family tradition handed down through generations

questions.q:
Five members of the Menon household do the things below. For each, write the value or idea from the chapter it shows, choosing from: dana (giving), seva (service), tyaga (sacrifice), cooperation (working together) and dharma (doing our duty). Use each one once.
(a) Before winter, the mother gives her old woollen shawls to the watchman's family.
(b) The elder sister spends every Sunday morning nursing her sick grandfather.
(c) The father gives up the new phone he was saving for, so the family can pay for the grandmother's operation.
(d) The whole family cleans the house together before Diwali.
(e) Twelve-year-old Ravi finishes the tasks he has been given at home every day without being reminded, because he sees them as his duty.
questions.a: (a) Dana (giving). (b) Seva (service). (c) Tyaga (sacrifice). (d) Cooperation (working together). (e) Dharma (doing our duty).
s: (a) Dana
(b) Seva
(c) Tyaga
(d) Cooperation
(e) Dharma

questions.q: Why did Shalini get a simple cotton dress for Onam instead of the silk dress she had expected?
questions.a: Her parents also bought new clothes for her uncle's family, who were in financial difficulty.
o: Her parents also bought new clothes for her uncle's family, who were in financial difficulty.
Her father's small business had closed down just before the family could go shopping for Onam.
Acchamma told her that silk dresses should not be worn during the festival of Onam.
Her mother wanted to save that money for unexpected needs in the future.

questions.q: In Shalini's story, who is Acchamma?
questions.a: Her father's mother

questions.q: A teacher wants to use Shalini's story, and only that story, to illustrate a point. Which point could the story of Shalini NOT be used to show?
questions.a: Parents discussing special expenses together before spending
o: Parents discussing special expenses together before spending
A grandparent helping a child understand why families share things
A family sharing what it has with members in difficulty
A child giving up something she wanted for others

questions.q:
Read the statements comparing the chapter's two family stories.
I. Both Shalini and Tenzing live with at least one grandparent.
II. In both stories, a change in a family member's work led to a change in what the family did at home.
III. In both stories, a grandfather helps the child with homework.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: True or False? 'Tenzing's father joined in the household chores after Tenzing's mother became busy in a local handicraft cooperative.' Give the verdict and a detail from the story that supports your answer.
questions.a: True. After his mother became busy in the handicraft cooperative, his father joined in cleaning the house, looking after the small vegetable garden and other chores, and often helps the grandmother prepare food.
s: Verdict: True
Supports it with a detail: cleaning, the vegetable garden, other chores or helping grandmother cook

questions.q: State one way in which Tenzing's grandmother, and one way in which his grandfather, contributes to Tenzing's life, as Tenzing describes them.
questions.a: Grandmother: she tells him interesting stories with humour and wisdom (and the father helps her cook food for everyone). Grandfather: he helps Tenzing with his homework and takes him to the school bus stop.
s: Grandmother: tells stories with humour and wisdom (or prepares food for the family)
Grandfather: helps with homework or takes him to the school bus stop

questions.q: Write a short situation of three or four lines, not taken from the chapter, in which a family changes who does the housework in the same way that Tenzing's family did. Then point out two details in your situation that match Tenzing's story.
questions.a: Sample: 'In Sneha's home in Nagpur, her mother starts working at a tailoring unit from morning to evening. Her father, who runs a cycle shop, now sweeps the house and waters the plants, and helps Sneha's grandmother cook dinner.' Matching details: (1) the mother becomes busy with work outside the home, as Tenzing's mother did with the handicraft cooperative; (2) the father takes on household chores and helps the grandmother cook, as Tenzing's father did.
s: Writes a fitting situation in which one member becomes busy with work outside the home
Shows another member (e.g. the father) taking on household chores in response
Names two matching details with Tenzing's story

questions.q:
Arrange the members of Shalini's household by generation, as you would in a family tree.
(a) Name the member of the oldest generation.
(b) Name the four members of the middle generation.
(c) Name the three members of the youngest generation.
(d) Which member of the youngest generation is Shalini's cousin in English terms, and what would she usually be called in most Indian languages?
questions.a: (a) Acchamma, the grandmother. (b) Shalini's father, her mother, Chittappa (her paternal uncle) and Chitti (her aunt). (c) Shalini, her younger brother and Chinni. (d) Chinni is her cousin in English; in most Indian languages she would simply be called her sister.
s: (a) Acchamma
(b) Father, mother, Chittappa and Chitti
(c) Shalini, her younger brother and Chinni
(d) Chinni; called a sister in most Indian languages

questions.q:
The Boro family lives in a village near Guwahati: a grandmother, the father, the mother and two children, Anu (12) and Bikash (9). The mother has joined a weaving cooperative. Before that she spent 2 hours a day cooking and 1 hour a day washing clothes. Now the father, who runs a tea stall, cooks with the grandmother, and Anu does the washing. This month the family has Rs 6,000 left after paying for food and clothing. The father wants to spend Rs 4,500 on a bicycle for Anu, whose school is 5 km away.
(a) Which family in the chapter made a similar change at home, and which member of that family took on the chores?
(b) How many hours of the mother's earlier housework in a 7-day week are now done by others?
(c) Anu now does the washing. Which idea in the chapter about children growing up does this show?
(d) Following how Tenzing's parents handle special expenses and his mother's advice, how should the Boros decide about the bicycle? How much would remain for unexpected needs if they buy it?
questions.a: (a) Tenzing's family in Meghalaya; his father took on the cleaning, the vegetable garden and other chores and helps the grandmother cook. (b) (2 + 1) x 7 = 21 hours a week. (c) As children grow up they take on more responsibilities in the home to help other family members. (d) The bicycle is a special expense, so the father should not decide alone: the parents should discuss it together, as Tenzing's parents do, keeping in mind the advice to save money for unexpected needs. If they buy it, Rs 6,000 - Rs 4,500 = Rs 1,500 remains; they may buy it because Anu's school is 5 km away and some money is still saved, or wait and save more, as long as the decision is made together.
s: (a) Tenzing's family; his father
(b) 21 hours
(c) Children take on more responsibilities at home as they grow up
(d) Parents decide together, weighing saving for unexpected needs; Rs 1,500 left if bought

questions.q:
Analyse what each of these people does in the chapter's two family stories, and which value or idea from the chapter it shows.
(a) Acchamma
(b) Shalini's parents
(c) Shalini
(d) Tenzing's father
(e) Tenzing's mother
questions.a: (a) Acchamma tells Shalini's father about his brother's money trouble and explains to Shalini that this is how families support each other and share what they have: the family as a 'school' where children learn values. (b) Shalini's parents buy new Onam clothes for Chittappa, Chitti and Chinni as well as for themselves: sharing and supporting members in difficulty (giving, dana). (c) Shalini settles for a cotton dress instead of the silk one and is happy everyone got new clothes: giving up her own wish for the family's needs (tyaga). (d) Tenzing's father takes on cleaning, the garden and other chores, and helps the grandmother cook, once the mother is busy: cooperation and interdependence, roles changing as needs change. (e) Tenzing's mother works in a handicraft cooperative, discusses special expenses with the father and advises saving for unexpected needs: sharing responsibility for the family's future.
s: (a) Acchamma: raises the uncle's need and explains family sharing (family as a school of values)
(b) Parents: buy clothes for the uncle's family, sharing/giving
(c) Shalini: accepts the cotton dress gladly, giving up her own wish (tyaga)
(d) Tenzing's father: takes on chores, cooperation/interdependence
(e) Tenzing's mother: works in the cooperative, discusses expenses, advises saving for the future

questions.q: According to the chapter, what may a group of families connected with one another and with the people around them be called?
questions.a: A community

questions.q: Which of these is an example of the kind of 'rules' on shared natural resources that the chapter describes?
questions.a: An unwritten village understanding that firewood is taken from the common forest only after the monsoon
o: An unwritten village understanding that firewood is taken from the common forest only after the monsoon
A printed notice in a city housing society saying that all pets must be kept on a leash in the lobby
A family's own rule that the children must finish their homework before they go out to play in the evening
A shopkeeper's rule that customers must pay in cash for everything they buy on credit days

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A family that refuses to do its share of cleaning the village's shared pond can affect the whole community.
Reason (R): The chapter says that the practices on the use of shared resources were usually written down as laws.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each term (Column A) with its description in the chapter (Column B).
Column A: 1. Community 2. Joint family 3. Nuclear family 4. 'Rules' on shared resources
Column B: A. A couple and their children, or sometimes one parent and children B. Practices agreed upon over time, rarely written down C. A group of connected families and people D. Several generations living together
True or False? 'The chapter says that the word community can have other meanings as well, depending on the context.' Give the verdict and the meaning of community that the chapter uses first.
questions.a: True. The chapter says there are other meanings for 'community' depending on the context; the meaning it uses first is a group of connected people, families connected with other families and the people around them.
s: Verdict: True
Gives the first meaning: a group of connected families and people around them

questions.q: What is a community, as the chapter first describes it? Give one reason, from the chapter, for which members of a community come together.
questions.a: A community is a group of connected people: families connected not only within themselves but with other families and the people around them. They come together, for example, to celebrate festivals, to organise feasts, weddings and other events, or (in some villages) to help each other with land preparation, sowing and harvesting.
s: Describes a community as a group of families/people connected with one another
Gives one reason: festivals, feasts, weddings or other events, or farm work like sowing and harvesting

questions.q:
In a village in Rajasthan, an old understanding that no one ever wrote down lets each family graze its goats on the common land only on fixed days of the week.
(a) Which of the shared resources named in the chapter is this, and what does the chapter say we may call such practices?
(b) What does the chapter say such practices have provided to communities?
questions.a: (a) Grazing land; the chapter says we may call such practices 'rules', though they were rarely written down. (b) They have provided communities secure access to resources (and they also mean that every family has specific duties to perform).
s: (a) Grazing lands; such practices may be called 'rules'
(b) Secure access to resources

questions.q:
(a) Name two reasons, other than farm work, for which members of a community come together.
(b) Name two farm activities in which people in some villages support each other.
(c) Among which communities does the chapter say agreed practices on shared resources are found?
questions.a: (a) Any two: celebrating festivals, organising feasts, weddings, other events. (b) Any two: land preparation, sowing, harvesting. (c) Among many tribal communities, and to some extent in village communities in rural India today.
s: (a) Two of: festivals, feasts, weddings, other events
(b) Two of: land preparation, sowing, harvesting
(c) Many tribal communities, and to some extent village communities in rural India today

questions.q: Gopal says: 'A community is only the people of a village who share land and water.' Check Gopal's claim against the chapter's section on community and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Gopal is only partly right. Villagers who share water, grazing lands and forest produce, with agreed practices and duties, are indeed a community in the chapter. But the chapter's meaning is wider: a community is any group of connected families and people, who come together for festivals, feasts, weddings and other events, not only to share land and water. The chapter also says 'community' has other meanings depending on the context, so it is not limited to a village.
s: Verdict: partly right; accepts that villagers sharing resources form a community
Shows the wider meaning: connected families coming together for festivals, feasts, weddings and events
Notes that the chapter says the word has other meanings depending on context, so it is not only a village

questions.q:
Hirapur is a village in Jharkhand with 24 families. Every June the families help one another prepare the land and sow paddy, and in October they harvest together. Water from the village's shared canal goes to one family's fields each day, in turn, so that every family gets one full day. An old understanding, never written down, also says that each family must clean the canal for one day each year. At Karam festival the whole village shares a feast.
(a) Name one farm activity in the passage that the chapter also mentions villagers helping each other with.
(b) After how many days does a family get its canal water again?
(c) What does the chapter say we may call an unwritten understanding like the one about the canal?
(d) One family stops cleaning the canal on its day. What does the chapter say happens if families do not perform their duties?
questions.a: (a) Any one: land preparation, sowing or harvesting. (b) There are 24 families and one day each, so a family gets water again after 24 days. (c) 'Rules', though they were rarely written down. (d) Shared access to resources means all families have specific duties to perform; otherwise the community will not function smoothly.
s: (a) Land preparation, sowing or harvesting
(b) 24 days
(c) 'Rules' (rarely written down)
(d) Every family has specific duties; otherwise the community will not function smoothly

questions.q: Which community followed its halma tradition to deal with the water crisis in the region around Jhabua?
questions.a: The Bhil community

questions.q: What did the region around the town of Jhabua, in Madhya Pradesh, suffer from year after year?
questions.a: An acute water crisis
o: Floods that turned roads into rivers

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the Bhils' work around Jhabua is an example of community action and not of one family's effort?
questions.a: Many people across hundreds of villages worked unpaid, as a duty to their community and the environment.
o: Many people across hundreds of villages worked unpaid, as a duty to their community and the environment.
One large family dug trenches only around its own fields, to protect its own crops from the dry summers.
The villagers were paid wages to plant trees, so many families joined to earn extra money that year.
The Bhils celebrated a festival each year, and planting trees was the main ritual of that festival.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Padma Shri award of 2019 was given to the whole Bhil community for planting trees around Jhabua.
Reason (R): In the halma tradition, the objective is to serve Mother Earth.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: What is the halma tradition, as the chapter describes it? Name one thing the Bhil community did around Jhabua by following it.
questions.a: Halma is the tradition of coming together to support any individual or family in times of crisis (its objective is to serve Mother Earth). Following it, the Bhils planted thousands of trees in hundreds of villages, and dug trenches and other water harvesting structures to conserve rainwater.
s: Halma: coming together to support any individual or family in times of crisis
One action: planting thousands of trees, or digging trenches/water harvesting structures

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says the Bhils worked 'as their duty towards their community and the environment'. Which principle, called earlier in the chapter an important principle of Indian culture, does this match?
(b) The spiritual and religious groups in the Chennai floods cooked and handed out food to people in need. Name one value from the family's 'school' of values (dana, seva or tyaga) that their action shows, and say why.
questions.a: (a) Following one's dharma, that is, doing one's duty. (b) Dana (giving), because they gave food to people who needed it without expecting anything in return; seva (service), because they served people in a crisis, is also accepted.
s: (a) Dharma, doing one's duty
(b) Dana (giving food) or seva (serving people in crisis), with a reason

questions.q:
(a) In which year did the Chennai floods described in the chapter take place?
(b) Name two problems the floods caused for people in the city.
(c) Who cooked large quantities of food and distributed it to people who needed it?
questions.a: (a) 2015. (b) Any two: roads turned to rivers; people could no longer move around; almost all shops were closed; services were interrupted. (c) Many private groups, in particular spiritual and religious organisations.
s: (b) Two of: roads turned to rivers, people could not move, shops closed, services interrupted
(c) Private groups, especially spiritual and religious organisations

questions.q:
Suppose that on one halma day in a village near Jhabua, 80 people each dig 2 trenches and 40 other people each plant 15 saplings.
(a) How many trenches and how many saplings are made that day?
(b) No one is paid. What reason does the chapter give for why the Bhils did such work without pay?
(c) What does the chapter say is the objective of the halma tradition?
questions.a: (a) 80 x 2 = 160 trenches and 40 x 15 = 600 saplings. (b) They did it as their duty towards their community and the environment. (c) To serve Mother Earth.
s: (a) 160 trenches and 600 saplings
(b) Duty towards the community and the environment
(c) To serve Mother Earth

questions.q:
Wadgaon, a hill village in Maharashtra, runs short of water every summer, when it needs about 15,000 litres a day. The villagers plan to dig 150 trenches on the slopes before the monsoon; each trench holds about 2,000 litres of rainwater when full. A contractor offers to dig all the trenches for Rs 200 per trench. An elder suggests that, as the Bhils did around Jhabua, 300 villagers dig them together over two Sundays without pay.
(a) Which tradition and which community from the chapter is the elder thinking of?
(b) How many litres can all the trenches hold when full?
(c) For how many days of summer need would one full filling last?
(d) Should Wadgaon hire the contractor or follow the elder's plan? Decide and justify using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The halma tradition of the Bhil community around Jhabua. (b) 150 x 2,000 = 3,00,000 litres. (c) 3,00,000 / 15,000 = 20 days. (d) The trenches store the same 3,00,000 litres either way. The contractor would cost 150 x Rs 200 = Rs 30,000. The elder's plan saves this money and, like halma, has the villagers come together without pay as a duty to their community and the environment, which also binds the village. Hiring is also defensible if the villagers cannot spare the time, but it costs Rs 30,000 and loses the community effort; a reasoned choice using the cost and the chapter earns the mark.
s: (a) The halma tradition of the Bhil community
(b) 3,00,000 litres
(c) 20 days
(d) Decides, using the Rs 30,000 cost and the chapter's idea of unpaid community duty

questions.q: Two groups in a class must choose ONE example from the chapter for a poster titled 'Community care for the environment'. Group A wants the Bhils around Jhabua; Group B wants the relief work in the Chennai floods of 2015. Evaluate which example fits the title better. In your answer: (a) describe what the community did around Jhabua; (b) describe what the community did in Chennai; (c) say what each action protected or helped; (d) decide which fits the title and why; (e) say what the other example shows instead.
questions.a: (a) Around Jhabua, the Bhils, following halma, planted thousands of trees in hundreds of villages and dug trenches and other water harvesting structures to conserve rainwater, unpaid. (b) In Chennai, when roads turned to rivers and almost all shops were closed, private groups, especially spiritual and religious organisations, cooked large quantities of food and gave it to people in need. (c) The Jhabua work protected water and the land (trees, rainwater), while the Chennai work helped people survive a crisis by feeding them. (d) Jhabua fits the title better: the Bhils did it as a duty towards the environment, and the objective of halma is to serve Mother Earth. (e) The Chennai example shows community care for people in a crisis, given without expecting anything in return, rather than care for the environment.
s: (a) Describes the Bhils' tree planting and trenches/water harvesting
(b) Describes the Chennai groups cooking and distributing food
(c) Says Jhabua protected water and land, Chennai fed people
(d) Chooses Jhabua, citing duty to the environment / serving Mother Earth
(e) Says Chennai shows care for people in a crisis, not the environment

questions.q: In which city did Kamal Parmar start giving free evening tuition to underprivileged children?
questions.a: Ahmedabad

questions.q: The chapter lists groups of people of a particular religion, region, common work or interest as communities. Which of these groups from the chapter's list is held together by the work its members do, rather than by religion or region?
questions.a: Kerala's scientific community

questions.q:
Read the statements about Residents' Welfare Associations (RWAs) as the chapter describes them.
I. An RWA's rules are made by its office-bearers without the residents taking part.
II. An RWA depends on the trading community for supplies.
III. The chapter says that new types of community have emerged only in villages in the last 30 or 40 years.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only

questions.q:
Match each example from the chapter (Column A) with the description that fits it (Column B).
Column A: 1. A Residents' Welfare Association 2. Kamal Parmar's evening classes 3. The Bhil community near Jhabua 4. The National Cadet Corps
Column B: A. A community you may belong to within your school B. A new type of urban community that makes its own rules C. A rural community acting through the halma tradition D. One person's initiative in a city that grew as volunteers joined
True or False? 'Kamal Parmar was a schoolteacher who taught the street children during his school hours.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Kamal Parmar owned a small auto-fabrication workshop, and he taught the children from 5:30 to 9:30 pm every day, after his regular work hours (some local schoolteachers joined him later).
s: Verdict: False
Corrects it: he owned a small auto-fabrication workshop and taught from 5:30 to 9:30 pm after his work hours

questions.q:
One volunteer in Kamal Parmar's classes said, 'We went there to teach, instead we learnt a lot from them.'
(a) Which group of volunteers in the story did this speaker belong to?
(b) Using what a local schoolteacher observed about the classes, explain one thing the volunteers could have learnt from the children.
questions.a: (a) The older children who were attending regular schools and joined as volunteer teachers. (b) The teacher observed that the children had no proper benches, no 'silence zone' classrooms and heard noisy vehicles passing by, yet paid all their attention to the teachers; the volunteers could learn how much the children valued learning and how to concentrate even in poor conditions.
s: (a) The older children from regular schools who volunteered
(b) Uses the teacher's observation (no benches, noise, yet full attention) to name a lesson such as dedication to learning

questions.q:
The chapter says a group of people of a particular religion, region, common work or interest may be called a community. Say which of these bases holds each group below together, and give a reason for each.
(a) The Bengali families who have settled in Bengaluru
(b) The fishermen of a coastal village in Odisha
(c) A school's chess club
questions.a: (a) Region: they are bound by coming from the same region (Bengal), even while living in another city. (b) Common work: they all earn their living by fishing. (c) Interest: its members share an interest in chess; the chapter counts school clubs as communities.
s: (a) Region, with reason
(b) Common work, with reason
(c) Interest, with reason

questions.q: Raghav says: 'Kamal Parmar's classes show that community in a city works in exactly the same way as community in a village.' Check Raghav's claim against the chapter and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Raghav is only partly right. The chapter does use Kamal Parmar's story to show that community is also present in an urban context, people coming together for others' benefit, as in the village examples. But it says urban community 'may function a little differently'. Around Jhabua, a whole community acted together through its old halma tradition; in Ahmedabad, one workshop owner began the classes on his own initiative after his work hours, and teachers and older students joined him later as volunteers.
s: Verdict: partly right; community is present in the city too
Cites the chapter's point that urban community may function a little differently
Contrasts a whole community acting through tradition (halma) with one person's initiative that volunteers joined

questions.q: Suppose Kamal Parmar's evening classes, now attended by 150 children, need one volunteer teacher for every 25 children, and dinner costs Rs 20 per child. Kamal can spend Rs 2,400 a day on dinner from his workshop earnings. (a) How many volunteer teachers are needed? (b) What does dinner for all the children cost each day, and how much short is Kamal? (c) Name the two groups from the chapter's story who joined Kamal as volunteer teachers. (d) Plan P: give dinner only to as many children as Rs 2,400 covers. Plan Q: ask nearby shopkeepers to cover the shortfall. Which plan would you advise, using the chapter's idea that communities are interdependent?
questions.a: (a) 150 / 25 = 6 volunteer teachers. (b) 150 x Rs 20 = Rs 3,000 a day; Kamal is Rs 3,000 - Rs 2,400 = Rs 600 short. (c) Some teachers from a local school, and older children attending regular schools. (d) Plan Q: under Plan P, Rs 2,400 / Rs 20 = 120 children would eat and 30 would go without dinner. The chapter says communities are ultimately interdependent and everyone depends on a number of other people and communities, just as an RWA depends on the trading community; asking the local trading community to cover Rs 600 a day keeps dinner for all 150 children.
s: (a) 6 teachers
(b) Rs 3,000 a day; Rs 600 short
(c) Local schoolteachers and older students from regular schools
(d) Advises Plan Q, noting 30 children would miss dinner under Plan P and using interdependence (e.g. on the trading community)

questions.q:
Riya, aged 12, lives in Ahmedabad with her parents and her grandmother in a flat in a housing society that has a Residents' Welfare Association. At school she is in the National Cadet Corps and the drama club. Using the chapter, analyse the groups Riya belongs to:
(a) What type of family is Riya's, and why?
(b) Name two communities Riya belongs to at school, and say why the chapter would call them communities.
(c) How can Riya's family take part in the rules of their housing society?
(d) Give two ways in which Riya's RWA depends on other communities.
(e) The chapter ends by calling the family 'the foundation of human society' and community 'a bigger unit'. Explain what these two ideas mean for Riya.
questions.a: (a) A joint family, because three generations (grandmother, parents and Riya) live together; a nuclear family is limited to a couple and their children. (b) The National Cadet Corps and the drama club (her class too); the chapter says that in school you may be part of different communities, groups held together by a common interest or activity. (c) RWAs make their own rules, for example on waste management, cleanliness of common areas and pets, and the people living in the community take part in making them, so her family can help make and follow these rules. (d) It depends on the trading community for supplies and on municipal workers to handle waste. (e) Her family is the base where members support each other in their duties and tasks; her communities are bigger units in which people also do their best to support each other, and these communities in turn depend on others.
s: (a) Joint family, as three generations live together
(b) NCC and drama club (or class) as school communities, with reason
(c) Residents take part in making the RWA's rules on waste, cleanliness or pets
(d) Trading community for supplies; municipal workers for waste
(e) Family as the foundation of mutual support, community as a bigger unit of support, communities interdependent
